record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: Can techniques inspired by fail-stop or Byzantine-failure handling be adapted so that they become acceptable for peer-to-peer systems from both the performance and security standpoints, despite high message overhead, complexity, and the lack of secure complete pairwise connectivity?

evidence.quote: Further research will be necessary to make these or similar techniques acceptable from a performance and security standpoint in a P2P context.

artifact.category_tag: Byzantine fault tolerance in peer-to-peer systems
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) distributed system consisting of a large, dynamic set of autonomous nodes that join and leave the network without central coordination. Nodes communicate by message passing over an overlay network in which secure, complete pairwise connectivity among all participants is not available, individual nodes may exhibit fail-stop behavior (halting unexpectedly) or Byzantine behavior (deviating arbitrarily and possibly maliciously from the prescribed protocol), and message overhead and protocol complexity directly impact system performance.

Classical fault-tolerance techniques developed for fail-stop and Byzantine-failure models in tightly coupled distributed systems (such as state-machine replication via Byzantine agreement, quorum-based replication, and cryptographic group protocols) typically assume reliable channels, bounded participant sets, and authenticated all-to-all communication, and they incur high message and computational overhead.

Problem: Design protocols, or prove impossibility results, for adapting fail-stop and Byzantine-failure fault-tolerance techniques to the P2P setting described above so that the resulting mechanisms are simultaneously:
(i) acceptable in performance, i.e., the message complexity, latency, and computational cost scale to large dynamic populations of peers; and
(ii) acceptable in security, i.e., they tolerate a non-trivial fraction of Byzantine peers in the absence of secure complete pairwise connectivity.

Specifically, exhibit a Byzantine-tolerant P2P protocol that provides guarantees analogous to classical Byzantine agreement or replicated state machines while meeting (i) and (ii), or establish lower bounds showing such guarantees are unattainable in the P2P model.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction rather than a single precise conjecture. Substantial progress has been made on Byzantine fault tolerance in P2P/overlay networks (e.g., Castro–Liskov BFT, secure overlay routing by Castro et al., S-Chord, sybil-resilient DHTs, and more recent BFT protocols underlying blockchain systems), but no single result resolves the general goal of fully performant and secure adaptation. Status is best characterized as unknown / ongoing research.
